title: Using electricity safely
keyIdea: Some things plug into a socket in the wall. That is mains electricity, and it is strong enough to hurt you badly. Other things, like a torch or a remote, use small batteries, which are much weaker. Keep water away from plugs and switches, and dry wet hands first. Never put metal or fingers into a socket or a toaster. To unplug, switch off and pull the plug, not the cable. Tell a grown-up about a broken cable or too many plugs in one socket. Fly kites far away from power lines.

kid: A lamp has a cable and a plug. It gets electricity from the wall. A torch has batteries inside.
Electricity from the wall is very strong. It can hurt you badly. A small battery is weak and safe to hold.
Water and electricity do not mix. Dry your hands before you touch a plug or a switch.
Never poke a fork, a finger or a toy into a socket or a toaster. Tell a grown-up if a cable is broken. Fly your kite in an open park, far from power lines.
adult: In England, the Year 4 science unit on electricity asks children to name everyday appliances that run on electricity. Its guidance adds that pupils should be taught to work safely with electricity. This lesson brings that forward for 6 and 7 year olds, who already use switches, sockets and battery toys. The words to use are mains electricity, socket, plug, cable, switch, appliance, battery and electric shock.

The science behind the rules: mains electricity in the UK is about 230 volts (about 120 volts in the US). An AA battery is 1.5 volts. Tap water and wet skin let electricity into the body far more easily than dry skin. That is why UK bathrooms use pull-cord switches and have no ordinary sockets near the bath. Metal is a good conductor, so a fork in a plugged-in toaster can carry electricity straight to a hand. Power lines carry thousands of volts, and the electricity can jump a gap. A kite string does not have to touch the line to be dangerous.

Common mistakes to watch for: thinking a battery toy and a wall socket are the same, or that wet hands are fine if you are quick. Pulling a plug out by its cable strains the wires inside until they break. Too many adaptors in one socket can overheat and start a fire. Children also need to hear that small batteries are safe to hold but must never go in the mouth. A swallowed button battery can burn the throat within hours.

In the lab your child sorts six things into plug-in or battery, tests how strong a battery and a wall socket are, dries wet hands and moves a hairdryer away from the sink, spots three dangers in a kitchen, switches off and pulls a plug out the safe way, and drags a kite away from power lines. Every step works with big buttons as well as taps and drags. Read the Challenge aloud together.

familyTip: Walk round your home together and find three things that plug in and three that use batteries. Then show your child where the switch for each socket is, how to switch off before unplugging, and which grown-up to tell if a cable looks damaged.

visual.caption: Safe or not safe? Drag each one, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: plug or battery, battery against socket, water, kitchen dangers, unplugging safely and kites near power lines.

practice.prompt: Which one gets its electricity from a socket in the wall?
practice.hint: Look for the one with a cable and a plug.
practice.explain: A toaster has a cable and a plug, so it uses mains electricity. A torch and a remote use batteries.

practice.prompt: A torch needs 2 batteries. You have {n} torches. How many batteries do you need?
practice.hint: Count in 2s, once for each torch.
practice.explain: Each torch needs 2 batteries, so {n} torches need {=2*n} batteries.

practice.prompt: In the kitchen, {a} things plug in and {b} things use batteries. How many things is that in all?
practice.hint: Start at {a} and count on {b} more.
practice.explain: {a} plug-in things and {b} battery things make {=a+b} things.

practice.prompt: Your hands are wet from washing. You want to turn on the light. What do you do?
practice.hint: Does being quick stop the water carrying electricity?
practice.explain: Water can carry electricity to you, so dry your hands first. Being quick does not help.

pool.prompt: Which is stronger, so it can hurt you badly?
pool.hint: Think of the two bars in the lab. Which one was huge?
pool.explain: A wall socket gives over 100 volts. A torch battery gives about 1.5 volts, so it is safe to hold.

pool.prompt: How do you unplug a lamp the safe way?
choices: Switch off, then pull the plug
Pull it out while it is on
pool.hint: Which part do you hold, and what do you do first?
pool.explain: Switch off at the wall, then hold the plug and pull. Pulling the cable can break the wires inside.

pool.prompt: Your toast is stuck in the toaster. What do you do?
choices: Ask a grown-up to unplug it
Get it out with a fork
Shake it while it is on
pool.hint: Is metal a safe thing to put inside a toaster?
pool.explain: A metal fork can carry electricity to your hand. A grown-up must switch off and unplug the toaster first.

pool.prompt: Your kite is stuck in a power line. What do you do?
choices: Let go and tell a grown-up
pool.hint: Can the string carry electricity down to you?
pool.explain: Let go and tell a grown-up. The string can carry electricity, and you must never climb a pole or pylon.

pool.prompt: A remote needs 2 batteries. A toy car needs {k} batteries. How many batteries for both?
pool.hint: Start at 2 and count on {k} more.
pool.explain: 2 batteries for the remote and {k} for the car make {=2+k} batteries.

pool.prompt: You see a cable with the wires showing. What do you do?
choices: Do not touch it and tell a grown-up
Plug it in to see if it works
pool.hint: Is a broken cable safe to touch?
pool.explain: Bare wires can give you an electric shock. Do not touch it, and tell a grown-up so they can deal with it.

pool.prompt: There are {t} sockets in a room. {u} have a plug in. How many are empty?
pool.hint: Start at {t} and take away the {u} with plugs.

pool.prompt: Why should a hairdryer be kept away from the bath and the sink?
choices: Water can carry electricity to you
It makes the water too hot
It will dry up the water
pool.hint: Think about water and electricity together.
pool.explain: Water and electricity do not mix. Water can carry the electricity to you and give you a shock.

pool.prompt: Lots of plugs are pushed into one socket. Why is that a problem?
choices: It can get hot and start a fire
pool.hint: What happened to the crowded socket in the lab?
pool.explain: Too many plugs in one socket can overheat and start a fire. Ask a grown-up to unplug some.
